title: INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY
body:
The theory course. Every other course asks how to compute something; this one asks what can
be computed at all, and how much machine you need to do it. The whole thing is one ladder:
start with a machine that has no memory ([[Finite Automata]]), add a [[Stack]]
([[Pushdown Automata]]), add unlimited tape ([[Turing Machine]]), and at each rung, find a
language the machine below cannot recognise.

It is the most [[Proof]]-heavy COMP course, so [[DISCRETE MATH]] is the real prerequisite.
The payoff lands in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] as
[[NP-Complete]]ness, and in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] as the [[Finite State Machine]]s you
actually build out of flip-flops.

## Topics

### The objects

[[Alphabet]] · [[Strings]] · [[Languages]] · [[Proof]]

An [[Alphabet]] $\Sigma$ is a finite set of symbols, a string is a finite sequence of them,
and a language is a *set* of strings. That is the whole subject matter: every machine in this
course is a device for answering "is this string in this language?"

Proof technique matters as much as content. [[Proof By Contradiction]] and
[[Proof By Induction]] are the two you use constantly.

### Finite automata

[[Automata]] · [[Finite Automata]] · [[DFA]] · [[NFA]] · [[Regular Expressions]] ·
[[Regular Languages]] · [[Nondeterminism]]

A machine with a fixed number of states and no memory beyond the state it is in. A [[DFA]]
has exactly one transition per state-and-symbol; an [[NFA]] may have several, none, or
$\varepsilon$-moves. The surprise is that this buys no power: every NFA can be converted into
a DFA by the subset construction, and [[Regular Expressions]] describe exactly the same class.

### The pumping lemma

[[Pumping Lemma]]

The tool for proving a language is *not* regular. If a language is regular, every long enough
string can be split $xyz$ and the middle piece repeated any number of times while staying in
the language. Find a string where that fails and you have your contradiction, which is how
you show $\{a^n b^n\}$ needs more than a finite automaton.

### Grammars and pushdown automata

[[Context-Free Grammars]] · [[Pushdown Automata]] · [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] · [[Stack]]

Add a [[Stack]] and you can count. [[Context-Free Grammars]] generate the same languages that
[[Pushdown Automata]] recognise: matched brackets, nested structure, essentially every
programming-language syntax. The [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] is the ladder itself: regular ⊂
context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable.

### Turing machines and undecidability

[[Turing Machine]] · [[Undecidability]] · [[Godel's Theorem]] · [[Lambda Calculus]]

Unlimited tape, and now you have a model of *everything* a computer can do. The
Church-Turing thesis says nothing more powerful is coming, and [[Lambda Calculus]] is the
evidence: a completely different formalism with exactly the same power. Then
[[Undecidability]] shows even this machine has limits, because the halting problem cannot be solved
by any program, by diagonalisation.

### Complexity

[[NP-Complete]] · [[Time Complexity]] · [[Algorithm]]

The last step down from "impossible" to "possible but not practically". A problem in NP has
solutions that are cheap to *check*; [[NP-Complete]] problems are the hardest of those, and
reduction is the technique for proving membership.

### Other models

[[Cellular Automata]] · [[Simulation]]

## Core Facts to Know

- An [[Alphabet]] $\Sigma$ is a finite, non-empty set of symbols.
- A string is a finite sequence of symbols; $\varepsilon$ is the empty string.
- $\Sigma^*$ is the set of all strings over $\Sigma$, including $\varepsilon$.
- A [[Languages|language]] is any subset of $\Sigma^*$.
- A [[DFA]] has exactly one transition for every state–symbol pair.
- An [[NFA]] may have zero, one, or many transitions per symbol, plus $\varepsilon$-transitions.
- Every [[NFA]] has an equivalent [[DFA]], via the subset construction.
- A DFA built from an $n$-state NFA can need up to $2^n$ states.
- DFAs, NFAs, and [[Regular Expressions]] all describe exactly the [[Regular Languages]].
- Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation, star, intersection, and complement.
- The [[Pumping Lemma]] proves a language is **not** regular; it never proves one is.
- Using the pumping lemma is always a [[Proof By Contradiction]].
- $\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}$ is not regular, because a finite automaton cannot count unboundedly.
- A [[Pushdown Automata|pushdown automaton]] is a finite automaton plus a [[Stack]].
- [[Context-Free Grammars]] and pushdown automata describe the same class of languages.
- $\{a^n b^n\}$ is context-free; $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is not.
- Unlike finite automata, a *nondeterministic* PDA is strictly more powerful than a deterministic one.
- Programming language syntax is context-free; that is why parsers use a stack.
- A [[Turing Machine]] is a finite control plus an unbounded read/write tape.
- The Church-Turing thesis: anything effectively computable is computable by a Turing machine.
- [[Lambda Calculus]] has exactly the same computational power as a Turing machine.
- The halting problem is [[Undecidability|undecidable]]; no program can decide it for all inputs.
- Undecidability is proved by diagonalisation and self-reference.
- Decidable means some machine always halts with an answer; recognisable only guarantees halting on *yes*.
- The [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] runs regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable.
- Each level of the hierarchy corresponds to a machine with more memory than the one below.
- **P** is problems solvable in polynomial time; **NP** is problems *verifiable* in polynomial time.
- A problem is [[NP-Complete]] if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it.
- SAT was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin).
- To show a new problem is NP-complete, reduce a known NP-complete problem *to* it.
- Nobody knows whether P = NP.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]], the prerequisite: [[Proof]], [[Sets]], [[Induction]],
  [[Proof By Contradiction]], [[Direct Proof]].
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: [[NP-Complete]] arrives there as [[Hamiltonian Cycle]];
  [[Stack]] and [[Graph]] are the concrete versions of the machinery here.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: carries P vs NP and [[Time Complexity]] further.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]]: [[Finite State Machine]]s as actual circuits rather than
  as mathematics.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]]: [[Lambda Calculus]] is where functional programming comes from.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Turing Machine]], [[Chomsky Hierarchy]],
  [[Regular Languages]], [[Nondeterminism]], [[Godel's Theorem]], [[Cellular Automata]].
